summary: This National Geographic Education encyclopedic entry explains wind energy, also called wind power, which uses a wind turbine to convert the wind's kinetic energy into electricity. It describes the two main turbine types (HAWTs and VAWTs), turbine sizes and output, how electricity is used or stored, and the U.S. turbine count. It closes with the Walney Extension, described as the largest offshore wind farm in the world.
one_line: National Geographic encyclopedic entry on how wind turbines convert wind's kinetic energy into electricity, turbine types, sizes, storage, and the Walney Extension offshore farm.
key_facts: Wind energy, or wind power, is created using a wind turbine, a device that channels the power of the wind to generate electricity.
The wind blows the blades of the turbine, which are attached to a rotor; the rotor then spins a generator to create electricity.
There are two types of wind turbines: horizontal-axis wind turbines (HAWTs) and vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs).
HAWTs are the most common type of wind turbine and usually have two or three long, thin blades that look like an airplane propeller.
VAWTs have shorter, wider curved blades that resemble the beaters used in an electric mixer.
Small, individual wind turbines can produce 100 kilowatts of power, enough to power a home.
Slightly larger wind turbines sit on towers as tall as 80 meters (260 feet) with rotor blades extending approximately 40 meters (130 feet) long and can generate 1.8 megawatts of power.
Even larger wind turbines stand on towers 240 meters (787 feet) tall with rotor blades more than 162 meters (531 feet) long and can generate anywhere from 4.8 to 9.5 megawatts of power.
The United States Department of Energy is working with the National Laboratories to develop technologies such as batteries and pumped-storage hydropower to store excess wind energy.
Companies like General Electric install batteries along with their wind turbines so that electricity can be stored right away as it is generated.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, there are 57,000 wind turbines in the United States, both on land and offshore.
A wind farm is a cluster of wind turbines and can generate enough electricity to power thousands of homes.
The Walney Extension is the largest offshore wind farm in the world, located in the Irish Sea approximately 19 kilometers (11 miles) west of the northwest coast of England.
The Walney Extension covers 149 square kilometers (56 square miles) and has a grid of 87 wind turbines standing 195 meters (640 feet) tall.
The Walney Extension has the potential to generate 659 megawatts of power, enough to supply 600,000 homes in the United Kingdom.
